name: Schisandra chinensis

lead: Schisandra is a vine whose berries are used as a tonic in Chinese, Korean and Russian traditions and sold as an adaptogen supplement.
Laboratory studies report liver-protective, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects. Human trials are small, often of multi-herb formulas, and none addresses appearance.

paras: Its lignans, such as schisandrin and schisandrin B, are reported in animal and cell studies to act on inflammatory and metabolic signalling, including AMPK/mTOR pathways.
Safety and interaction data are not well covered in the sources reviewed. Product identity can vary because S. chinensis and S. sphenanthera are different species.

lead: Schisandra chinensis, the Chinese magnolia vine or five-flavour berry (wuweizi in Chinese, omija in Korean), is a deciduous woody vine native to forests of northern China, the Russian Far East, Korea and Japan.[1] Its red berries are used in traditional medicine and in a Korean cordial drink, and the extract is sold as an adaptogen in the longevity-supplement category.[1][2]

The berries contain lignans such as schisandrin, deoxyschizandrin and gomisins.[1][3] A 2008 review summarises Russian research on the plant as a tonic and stimulant, and laboratory studies report liver-protective, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects.[2][4][5][6][7]
Human evidence is sparse. No study found in these sources tests schisandra for facial appearance, skin or hair outcomes.
infobox: S. sphenanthera, distinguished in the 2015 Chinese Pharmacopoeia[1]

paras: The Chinese and Korean names both refer to the berry's five flavours: bitter, sweet, sour, salty and pungent.[1] Wikipedia notes the Ainu used the plant as a remedy for colds and sea-sickness, and that Koreans make the berries into the cordial omija-cha.[1] The genus was published by André Michaux in 1803, and the plant was once placed in Magnoliaceae, hence the name Chinese magnolia vine.[1]

Reviews list dibenzocyclooctadiene lignans as the characteristic constituents of the fruit and describe analytical methods that distinguish S. chinensis from S. sphenanthera.[3][8] Preclinical studies report that schisandrin has anti-inflammatory effects in cell models,[6] that schisandrin B promotes fatty-acid oxidation and reduces liver fat accumulation in a mouse model through AMPK/mTOR signalling,[7] and that pollen extract and an acidic polysaccharide reduced chemically induced liver injury in mice.[4][5] A 2008 review of Russian research covers its traditional use as a general tonic.[2]

Registered human trials are few and small. They include a 54-person randomised trial of extract on musculoskeletal biomarkers in relatively sarcopenic adults,[9] a Phase 2/3 study of omija extract in mild knee osteoarthritis (60),[10] a trial of a multi-herb formula in fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue syndrome that includes schisandra among six ingredients,[11] and a Phase 3 trial of the Shengmai San formula to prevent chemotherapy-related cardiac toxicity.[12] Another trial compared a combined Rhodiola, Schisandra and Eleutherococcus preparation with rhodiola extract and ginseng in employed middle-aged women.[13] The sources consulted give no results, and none tests an appearance outcome.
The sources consulted contain no safety or drug-interaction information specific to schisandra beyond the Russian-research review's coverage of its traditional use as a tonic.[2][1]
